title: Night prayers, the Qur'an, and iftar together
hook: Ten days in. Tonight: the night prayer, the Qur'an, and why you shouldn't break your fast alone.

screens.text: **About ten days in.** The hunger is easier now, right? Today is about the nights: the special night prayer, the Qur'an, and one thing that matters more than people admit: not breaking your fast alone.

variant.default: **Tarawih** (the night prayer of Ramadan) is prayed in congregation at the masjid after Isha. It isn't required, and it's loved: whoever prays Ramadan's nights with faith, hoping for Allah's reward, is forgiven their past sins [Bukhari 37].
variant.hanafi: **Tarawih** (the night prayer of Ramadan) is 20 rak'ahs (units), prayed two at a time after Isha, in congregation at the masjid. It's a strongly recommended sunnah, not an obligation.
hanafi_bubbles: Whoever prays Ramadan's nights with faith, hoping for Allah's reward, is forgiven their past sins [Bukhari 37].

bubbles: Some masjids pray 8 rak'ahs (units), some 20, two at a time. {{masjid.name}} will show you its practice.

screens.title: Tarawih behind the imam
screens.intro: **New? Tarawih is easier than it looks.** You don't need to know long surahs.

moves.text: Listen as he recites. {{masjid.name}} will show you what to say, and what to listen to.
Follow his movements: when he bows, you bow.
He ends with the salam after every two rak'ahs. Stay for two, eight, or all of it.
Behind the imam you don't recite al-Fatiha or a surah at all, not even quietly. You listen [Q 7:204].
Follow his movements, saying the phrases you know in each position.
He ends with the salam after every two rak'ahs. Stay for two, eight, or all twenty.

screens.prompt: Dre has work at 7 a.m. He can stay for 8 rak'ahs of tarawih, not 20. What should he do?

options.text: Pray the 8 and head home; that's real worship, and he can add more on a weekend
options.feedback: Right. Tarawih isn't required, and every rak'ah counts. Doing what he can keep up is the way.

options.text: Skip it, since he can't finish
options.feedback: Not quite. Part of it is far better than none. Every rak'ah he prays counts.

options.text: Skip Isha so he can stay for all of tarawih another night
options.feedback: Not quite. Isha is required; tarawih isn't. Isha always comes first.

screens.text: **The month of the Qur'an.** The Qur'an was first sent down in Ramadan [Q 2:185], so Muslims spend extra time with it now.

screens.situation: Hannah wants a Qur'an goal for the rest of Ramadan. She works full time. Which goal fits?

options.text: A page of translation a day, or listening to a recitation on her commute
options.feedback: Yes. Pick a goal you'll keep. Spending time with the Qur'an is the point.

options.text: Finish the whole book by Eid, even if she has to skip sleep
options.feedback: Not quite. Finishing the whole book isn't the point. Spending time with it is.

options.text: Wait until after Ramadan, when she has more time
options.feedback: Not quite. This is the month of the Qur'an. Even a page a day counts.

screens.before: In a 2025 survey of 618 American converts,
screens.after: said they felt lonely at Ramadan or Eid [Yaqeen 2025].

options.feedback: Yes, 40%. Breaking your fast alone in your car or your room is really common, and it's hard.
Not quite. It was 40%. If you've felt lonely this month, you're far from alone.
Not quite. It was 40%: a lot of converts, and a real need.

screens.text: **Here's the good news:** whoever feeds a fasting person gets the same reward as their fast [Tirmidhi 807]. Your masjid *wants* to feed you.

screens.situation: Keisha has broken every fast this week alone in her apartment. The masjid hosts a free community iftar every evening, but she doesn't know anyone and feels awkward walking in.

options.text: Message her mentor and ask to meet at the masjid iftar tonight, so she has someone to sit with
options.feedback: Yes. One familiar face makes the door easy. Mentors want this message.

options.text: Keep eating alone; she'll go next year when she knows people
options.feedback: Understandable, but this is how people get to know each other. Next year starts tonight.

options.text: Go, but leave right after the dates without talking to anyone
options.feedback: Better than not going! Next step: stay for the meal and ask one person their name.

screens.character: A friendly regular at the masjid's community iftar, about your age and gender, who's been coming for years. Warm, a little chatty. Never pushy or preachy.
screens.setup: You've just sat down at a long table at the masjid iftar with your plate. The person next to you smiles: "Hey, I don't think I've seen you before. Is this your first time here?"
screens.goal: Introduce yourself, say you're new to Islam (only if you want to), and make one real connection.
screens.success_looks_like: You give your name, answer simply, ask them a question back, and maybe swap numbers or agree to sit together again.
screens.coach_notes: The regular asks friendly questions: 'Where are you from?', 'How's your fasting going?', 'Are you coming to tarawih?'. They're delighted if the convert shares they're new, and never quiz them on religion or push marriage, a madhab or anything heavy. If the convert prefers not to say they're new, the regular doesn't push. Debrief: praise any question they asked back; suggest one easy line for next time.

You weren't meant to do Ramadan alone. Someone at that table is glad you came.

options.text: No. It's a strongly recommended night prayer; pray what you can
options.feedback: Right. It's loved and rewarded [Bukhari 37], but not required like Isha.

options.text: Yes, all of it, every night
options.feedback: Not quite. It isn't required. Every rak'ah you pray counts.

check.prompt: Why are masjids happy to feed you at iftar?

options.text: Feeding a fasting person earns the reward of their fast
options.feedback: Right. The one who feeds a fasting person shares their reward [Tirmidhi 807].

aiContext:
**Lesson facts**
- Praying Ramadan's nights with faith and hope of reward brings forgiveness of past sins [Bukhari 37]. Tarawih: Hanafi, 20 rak'ahs in pairs after Isha and before witr [First Instructions Part II]; a confirmed sunnah in the Hanafi school. Many masjids pray 8; both are practiced.
- Hanafi: the follower doesn't recite behind the imam, in any prayer; he listens [Q 7:204] and says the other phrases (takbirs, tasbih, tashahhud) himself.
- The Qur'an was first revealed in Ramadan [Q 2:185].
- Feeding a fasting person earns the reward of their fast [Tirmidhi 807, sahih per al-Albani].
- Yaqeen 2025 (618 US converts): 40% lonely at Ramadan or Eid; Muslim friends and mosque attachment were the strongest predictors of staying strong in faith.

**Likely questions**
- *"Masjid iftar etiquette?"* Arrive a few minutes before sunset; men and women often sit in separate areas; dates and water first, then Maghrib in congregation, then the meal. It's fine to say "I'm new." Offer to help clean up: it's the fastest way to meet people.
- *"How do I follow in tarawih?"* Line up, intend tarawih, follow the imam; it's prayed in pairs. Witr is prayed after it in congregation in Ramadan at Hanafi masjids; Day 8 taught witr. Leaving early is fine.
- *"Where to start with the Qur'an?"* A good English translation (Saheeh International, or one the masjid recommends), starting with short surahs or al-Baqarah's fasting verses (2:183–187). Audio with translation works for busy people.
- *"I feel lonely."* Normalize it (40% stat), then one concrete step: message the mentor, go to an iftar, join a class. Watch for signs of something heavier (safety rule).

**Escalate:** anything suggesting depression or self-harm (safety rule); a teen who can't get to the masjid without parents' knowledge (mentor; safeguarding: in-person meetings in public masjid spaces, mentor of the same gender, second adult included).

**Don't**
- Don't make tarawih sound required or shame anyone for leaving early.
- Don't pressure a convert to announce they're new.
- Don't settle the 8-vs-20 debate beyond "both are practiced; follow your masjid."

**Role-play brief:** A friendly iftar regular. Asks easy questions, delighted to meet someone new, never preachy or pushy. Debrief on asking a question back and one easy line for next time.
madhabNote:
- **How many rak'ahs:** the classical practice in the four schools is 20 rak'ahs (the Maliki school also records a longer practice from Madinah). Many masjids today pray 8. All agree it's a sunnah, not an obligation.
- **Reciting behind the imam:** in the Hanafi school the follower stays silent; the Shafi'i school has the follower recite al-Fatiha. Follow {{masjid.name}}'s teaching.
